metadata.jurisdiction: Supreme Court of India / High Courts / Tribunals
metadata.annotation_method: Multi-tier dual legal curation using official Indian Supreme Court and statutory texts; independent verification of citations, factual points, and negative controls.
metadata.dataset_limitations: Benchmark covers landmark Constitution Bench decisions, Division Bench rulings, and major commercial statutes. Ongoing pilot expansion tracks state-specific High Court splits and tribunal decrees.

corpus.text: Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act provides that when a contract is broken, if a sum is named as liquidated damages, the party complaining of the breach is entitled to receive reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount so named. In Kailash Nath Associates v. Delhi Development Authority (2015), the Supreme Court held that proof of actual loss is essential to award liquidated damages under Section 74, except in rare cases where loss is impossible or difficult to prove.

metadata.case_name: Kailash Nath Associates v. DDA

corpus.text: In Kailash Nath Associates, DDA had forfeited the earnest money of Rs. 78 lakhs deposited by the appellant upon alleged failure to pay the remaining auction price. The Supreme Court found that DDA subsequently re-auctioned the plot for Rs. 11.78 crores—far higher than the appellant's bid of Rs. 3.12 crores. Since DDA suffered no loss, forfeiture of earnest money under Section 74 was held unlawful and arbitrary.

metadata.case_name: Kailash Nath Associates v. DDA

corpus.text: In ONGC v. Saw Pipes Ltd (2003) 5 SCC 705, the Supreme Court held that if the terms of the contract are clear and unambiguous regarding genuine pre-estimated damages, the court is competent to award the stipulated sum without calling upon the party to prove actual loss. The court also held that patent illegality in an arbitral award constitutes a violation of public policy under Section 34 of the Arbitration Act.

metadata.case_name: ONGC v. Saw Pipes Ltd

corpus.text: In Associate Builders v. Delhi Development Authority (2015) 3 SCC 49, the Supreme Court clarified the scope of 'public policy of India' under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996. It held that an arbitral award can be set aside only on grounds such as fundamental policy of Indian law, interest of India, justice or morality, or patent illegality appearing on the face of the award. The court emphasized that the merits of an award cannot be re-opened in a Section 34 petition.

metadata.case_name: Associate Builders v. DDA

corpus.text: In Ssangyong Engineering & Construction Co. Ltd. v. NHAI (2019) 15 SCC 131, the Supreme Court examined the 2015 Amendment to Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act. The court followed Associate Builders but ruled that after the 2015 amendment, 'patent illegality' is no longer available to challenge international commercial arbitrations seated in India, and the test of public policy is strictly narrowed to fundamental policy of Indian law and basic notions of morality or justice.

metadata.case_name: Ssangyong Engineering & Construction v. NHAI

corpus.text: In Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017) 10 SCC 1, a unanimous nine-judge Constitution Bench held that the Right to Privacy is a fundamental right guaranteed under Article 21 and Part III of the Constitution. The court expressly overruled previous judgments in M.P. Sharma (1954) and Kharak Singh (1964) to the extent that they held privacy was not a constitutionally protected right.

metadata.case_name: Puttaswamy v. Union of India

corpus.text: In Puttaswamy, the court established a strict three-fold proportionality test for any state encroachment upon privacy: (i) legality (existence of a law), (ii) legitimate state aim or need, and (iii) proportionality of the means adopted to the object sought to be achieved, ensuring the measure is the least intrusive option.

metadata.case_name: Puttaswamy v. Union of India

corpus.text: In M.P. Sharma v. Satish Chandra (1954) SCR 1077, an eight-judge bench held that search warrants under Section 96 of the Code of Criminal Procedure did not violate Article 19(1)(f) or Article 20(3) of the Constitution, observing that the Indian Constitution does not recognize an express fundamental right to privacy analogous to the Fourth Amendment of the US Constitution.

metadata.case_name: M.P. Sharma v. Satish Chandra

corpus.text: In Kharak Singh v. State of U.P. (1964) 1 SCR 332, a six-judge bench held that unauthorized domiciliary police visits at night violated personal liberty under Article 21, but the majority rejected the existence of a broader fundamental right to privacy. Subba Rao, J. in his dissenting opinion held that privacy was an integral element of personal liberty.

metadata.case_name: Kharak Singh v. State of U.P.

corpus.text: In Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India (1996) 5 SCC 647, the Supreme Court integrated the 'Precautionary Principle' and the 'Polluter Pays Principle' into Indian environmental jurisprudence as essential features of sustainable development under Article 21 of the Constitution. The court held that polluting tanneries must pay compensation to affected citizens and fund environmental remediation.

metadata.case_name: Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. UOI

corpus.text: In M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Oleum Gas Leak Case) (1987) 1 SCC 395, the Supreme Court articulated the doctrine of 'Absolute Liability' for hazardous and inherently dangerous industrial enterprises. The court expressly distinguished the English rule of Strict Liability in Rylands v. Fletcher (1868), ruling that absolute liability is not subject to any exceptions such as act of God or third-party interference.

metadata.case_name: M.C. Mehta v. Union of India

corpus.text: In P. Chidambaram v. Central Bureau of Investigation (2019) 9 SCC 24, the Supreme Court laid down the judicial 'Triple Test' for regular bail under Section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure: (1) flight risk, (2) tampering with evidence, and (3) influencing witnesses. The court reiterated that bail is the rule and jail is the exception even in economic offences, unless the triple test is breached.

metadata.case_name: P. Chidambaram v. CBI

corpus.text: In Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab (1980) 2 SCC 684, the Constitution Bench upheld the constitutional validity of capital punishment under Section 302 IPC, but circumscribed its imposition strictly to the 'rarest of rare cases' where the alternative option of life imprisonment is unquestionably foreclosed. The court mandated balancing aggravating circumstances of the crime against mitigating circumstances of the offender.

metadata.case_name: Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab

corpus.text: In Machhi Singh v. State of Punjab (1983) 3 SCC 470, the Supreme Court applied and structured the Bachan Singh rarest of rare doctrine into five clear categories: (i) manner of commission of murder (extreme brutality), (ii) motive (depravity/hire), (iii) antisocial nature (bride burning/caste massacre), (iv) magnitude of crime (mass murders), and (v) personality of victim (child/defenseless).

metadata.case_name: Machhi Singh v. State of Punjab

corpus.text: In State of Punjab v. Ram Singh Ex-Constable (1992) 4 SCC 54, the Supreme Court interpreted Rule 16.2(1) of the Punjab Police Rules regarding dismissal for 'gravest acts of misconduct'. The court held that a single lapse or isolated negligent conduct does not automatically qualify as gravest misconduct; there must be intentional, willful disregard of duty or habitual delinquency.

metadata.case_name: State of Punjab v. Ram Singh

corpus.text: In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) 4 SCC 225, a thirteen-judge Constitution Bench formulated the 'Basic Structure Doctrine'. The court held that Parliament has wide amending powers under Article 368 of the Constitution, but it cannot amend, alter, or damage the basic structure or essential framework of the Constitution.

metadata.case_name: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala

corpus.text: In Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) 1 SCC 248, the Supreme Court overruled the narrow interpretation of Article 21 from A.K. Gopalan (1950), ruling that 'procedure established by law' must not be arbitrary, oppressive, or fanciful; it must be just, fair, and reasonable. This introduced substantive due process principles into Indian constitutional law.

metadata.case_name: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India

corpus.text: Statutory Text - Section 74, Indian Contract Act 1872: 'Compensation for breach of contract where penalty stipulated for: When a contract has been broken, if a sum is named in the contract as the amount to be paid in case of such breach, or if the contract contains any other stipulation by way of penalty, the party complaining of the breach is entitled, whether or not actual damage or loss is proved to have been caused thereby, to receive from the party who has broken the contract reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount so named or, as the case may be, the penalty stipulated for.'

metadata.case_name: Indian Contract Act, 1872

corpus.text: Statutory Text - Section 34(2), Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996: 'An arbitral award may be set aside by the Court only if: (b) the Court finds that: (ii) the arbitral award is in conflict with the public policy of India. Explanation 1: An award is in conflict with public policy only if: (i) it was induced by fraud or corruption; (ii) it is in contravention with the fundamental policy of Indian law; or (iii) it is in conflict with the most basic notions of morality or justice.'

metadata.case_name: Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996

corpus.text: Statutory Text - Section 439, Code of Criminal Procedure 1973: 'Special powers of High Court or Court of Session regarding bail: (1) A High Court or Court of Session may direct (a) that any person accused of an offence and in custody be released on bail, and if the offence is of the nature specified in sub-section (3) of section 437, may impose any condition which it considers necessary for the purposes of that sub-section.'

metadata.case_name: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973

corpus.text: In Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018) 10 SCC 1, a unanimous five-judge Constitution Bench decriminalized consensual sexual acts between adults in private by reading down Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code. The court held that Section 377 violated Articles 14, 15, 19(1)(a), and 21 of the Constitution. The court held that constitutional morality, not majoritarian morality, must guide judicial adjudication and expressly overruled its earlier decision in Suresh Kumar Koushal v. Naz Foundation (2014) 1 SCC 1.

metadata.case_name: Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India

corpus.text: In Suresh Kumar Koushal v. Naz Foundation (2014) 1 SCC 1, a two-judge bench of the Supreme Court overturned the Delhi High Court judgment and upheld the constitutional validity of Section 377 IPC. The court reasoned that homosexuals and transgender persons constitute only a minuscule fraction of the country's population and that Parliament, rather than the judiciary, is the appropriate body to amend or repeal penal statutes. This judgment was subsequently overruled in Navtej Singh Johar (2018).

metadata.case_name: Suresh Kumar Koushal v. Naz Foundation

corpus.text: In Joseph Shine v. Union of India (2019) 3 SCC 39, the Constitution Bench struck down Section 497 of the Indian Penal Code (adultery) and Section 198(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure as unconstitutional under Articles 14 and 21. The court ruled that Section 497 was based on archaic Victorian patriarchal notions treating the wife as chattel or property of the husband, depriving married women of autonomy, sexual agency, and equal constitutional status, overruling Sowmithri Vishnu (1985).

metadata.case_name: Joseph Shine v. Union of India

corpus.text: In A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950) SCR 88, a six-judge bench of the Supreme Court interpreted 'procedure established by law' in Article 21 literally as procedure prescribed by legislative enactment. The court held that fundamental rights in Part III operate in distinct watertight compartments (Articles 19 and 21 were mutually exclusive) and rejected substantive due process. This rigid doctrine was subsequently overruled in R.C. Cooper (1970) and Maneka Gandhi (1978).

metadata.case_name: A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras

corpus.text: In Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992) Supp (3) SCC 217 (Mandal Commission Case), a nine-judge Constitution Bench upheld 27% reservation for Other Backward Classes (OBCs) under Article 16(4) subject to the exclusion of the 'creamy layer'. The court established a strict 50% ceiling on total reservations, held that backward classes cannot be identified solely on the basis of economic criteria without social and educational backwardness, and ruled that Article 16(4) does not permit reservation in promotions.

metadata.case_name: Indra Sawhney v. Union of India

corpus.text: In M. Nagaraj v. Union of India (2006) 8 SCC 212, a five-judge Constitution Bench upheld the constitutional validity of Articles 16(4A) and 16(4B) providing for reservation in promotion with consequential seniority for SCs and STs. However, the court held that the State must place quantifiable data before providing promotion reservations demonstrating: (i) backwardness of the class, (ii) inadequacy of representation in service, and (iii) overall administrative efficiency under Article 335.

metadata.case_name: M. Nagaraj v. Union of India

corpus.text: Statutory Text - Article 21, Constitution of India 1950: 'Protection of life and personal liberty: No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law.'

metadata.case_name: Constitution of India, 1950

corpus.text: Statutory Text - Article 14, Constitution of India 1950: 'Equality before law: The State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India.'

metadata.case_name: Constitution of India, 1950

corpus.text: In Vidya Drolia v. Durga Trading Corporation (2021) 2 SCC 1, a three-judge bench of the Supreme Court held that landlord-tenant disputes governed by the Transfer of Property Act 1882 are arbitrable, overruling Himangni Enterprises (2017). The court articulated a four-fold test for non-arbitrable disputes: (i) disputes relating to actions in rem; (ii) disputes affecting third-party rights or erga omnes; (iii) disputes involving inalienable sovereign functions; and (iv) disputes expressly made non-arbitrable by statute.

metadata.case_name: Vidya Drolia v. Durga Trading Corporation

corpus.text: In NN Global Mercantile Pvt. Ltd. v. Indo Unique Flame Ltd. (2023) 7 SCC 1, a five-judge Constitution Bench held by a 3:2 majority that an unstamped or insufficiently stamped commercial contract containing an arbitration clause cannot be acted upon or enforced under Section 11 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996 until the instrument is impounded and validated under the Indian Stamp Act 1899. This decision was subsequently reconsidered and overruled by a seven-judge bench.

metadata.case_name: NN Global Mercantile v. Indo Unique Flame

corpus.text: In In Re: Interplay Between Arbitration Agreements and the Indian Stamp Act 1899 (2024) 6 SCC 1, a unanimous seven-judge Constitution Bench overruled NN Global (5-Judge) and held that non-stamping or insufficient stamping is a curable defect under the Stamp Act. The court held that an unstamped arbitration agreement is not void ab initio, and the referral court under Section 8 or 11 must examine only the prima facie existence of the agreement, leaving stamping objections to the arbitral tribunal under Section 16.

metadata.case_name: In Re: Interplay Between Arbitration and Stamp Act

corpus.text: In Bharat Aluminium Co. (BALCO) v. Kaiser Aluminium Technical Services Inc. (2012) 9 SCC 552, a five-judge Constitution Bench established the territoriality principle in Indian arbitration law, ruling that Part I of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996 does not apply to foreign-seated international commercial arbitrations. The court prospectively overruled Bhatia International (2002) and Venture Global (2008), holding that Indian courts have no jurisdiction to entertain Section 9 interim measures or Section 34 set-aside petitions against foreign awards.

metadata.case_name: BALCO v. Kaiser Aluminium

corpus.text: In Bhatia International v. Bulk Trading S.A. (2002) 4 SCC 105, a three-judge bench held that Part I of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996 applied to international commercial arbitrations held outside India unless the parties had expressly or impliedly excluded all or any of its provisions. This led to Indian courts granting interim injunctions and hearing set-aside challenges against foreign arbitral awards, until it was prospectively overruled by the Constitution Bench in BALCO (2012).

metadata.case_name: Bhatia International v. Bulk Trading S.A.

corpus.text: In National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) v. M. Hakeem (2021) 9 SCC 1, the Supreme Court held that the jurisdiction of a court under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996 is limited to either setting aside an arbitral award or remitting the matter to the arbitrator under Section 34(4). Section 34 does not confer any power on the court to modify, revise, or vary an arbitral award or substitute its own damages assessment for the award of the arbitrator.

metadata.case_name: NHAI v. M. Hakeem

corpus.text: Statutory Text - Section 8, Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996: 'Power to refer parties to arbitration where there is an arbitration agreement: (1) A judicial authority, before which an action is brought in a matter which is the subject of an arbitration agreement shall... refer the parties to arbitration unless it finds that prima facie no valid arbitration agreement exists.'

metadata.case_name: Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996

corpus.text: Statutory Text - Section 16, Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996: 'Competence of arbitral tribunal to rule on its jurisdiction: (1) The arbitral tribunal may rule on its own jurisdiction, including ruling on any objections with respect to the existence or validity of the arbitration agreement, and for that purpose— (a) an arbitration clause which forms part of a contract shall be treated as an agreement independent of the other terms of the contract.' (Kompetenz-Kompetenz Principle).

metadata.case_name: Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996

corpus.text: In Innoventive Industries Ltd. v. ICICI Bank (2018) 1 SCC 407, the Supreme Court laid down the definitive scheme for admission of insolvency applications under Section 7 of the IBC. The court held that the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT) must merely satisfy itself that a default of financial debt has occurred. Once a financial debt and default are established through records of an information utility or evidence, the corporate debtor cannot plead any dispute or set-off to resist admission, unlike in operational debt claims under Section 9.

metadata.case_name: Innoventive Industries v. ICICI Bank

corpus.text: In Swiss Ribbons Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India (2019) 4 SCC 17, the Supreme Court upheld the constitutional validity of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code 2016 in its entirety. The court held that the classification between financial creditors (who are involved in project finance and viability assessment) and operational creditors (who supply goods/services) is valid under Article 14 based on intelligible differentia. The primary objective of the IBC is corporate reorganization and resolution of viable companies, not debt recovery.

metadata.case_name: Swiss Ribbons v. Union of India

corpus.text: In Committee of Creditors of Essar Steel India Ltd. v. Satish Kumar Gupta (2020) 8 SCC 531, the Supreme Court firmly established the supremacy of the 'commercial wisdom' of the Committee of Creditors (CoC) in approving a resolution plan under Section 30(4) of the IBC. The court held that neither NCLT nor NCLAT possesses jurisdiction to sit in appeal over commercial decisions of the CoC or alter the negotiated distribution of proceeds between secured financial creditors and operational creditors, provided mandatory statutory minimums are satisfied.

metadata.case_name: CoC of Essar Steel v. Satish Kumar Gupta

corpus.text: In P. Mohanraj v. Shah Brothers ISPAT Pvt. Ltd. (2021) 6 SCC 258, the Supreme Court held that the statutory moratorium under Section 14(1)(a) of the IBC covers proceedings under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act 1881 for dishonor of cheques against the corporate debtor. The court clarified that the term 'proceedings' in Section 14 includes quasi-criminal proceedings that result in civil recovery. However, natural persons such as directors and signatories remain personally liable and are not protected by the corporate moratorium.

metadata.case_name: P. Mohanraj v. Shah Brothers ISPAT

corpus.text: In Vidarbha Industries Power Ltd. v. Axis Bank Ltd. (2022) 8 SCC 352, the Supreme Court held that Section 7(5)(a) of the IBC uses the word 'may', conferring judicial discretion upon the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT) to decline or defer admission of a financial creditor's Section 7 petition in exceptional circumstances, even when debt and default exist. In this case, where the corporate debtor held an enforceable arbitral award against a state entity exceeding its total financial debt, mechanical initiation of CIRP was held inappropriate.

metadata.case_name: Vidarbha Industries Power v. Axis Bank

corpus.text: Statutory Text - Section 7, Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code 2016: 'Initiation of corporate insolvency resolution process by financial creditor: (1) A financial creditor either by itself or jointly with other financial creditors... may file an application for initiating corporate insolvency resolution process against a corporate debtor before the Adjudicating Authority when a default has occurred. (5) Where the Adjudicating Authority is satisfied that— (a) a default has occurred and the application under sub-section (2) is complete... it may, by order, admit such application.'

metadata.case_name: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016

corpus.text: Statutory Text - Section 14, Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code 2016: 'Moratorium: (1) Subject to provisions of sub-sections (2) and (3), on the insolvency commencement date, the Adjudicating Authority shall by order declare moratorium for prohibiting all of the following, namely: (a) the institution of suits or continuation of pending suits or proceedings against the corporate debtor including execution of any judgment, decree or order in any court of law, tribunal, arbitration panel or other authority; (b) transferring, encumbering, alienating or disposing of by the corporate debtor any of its assets.'

metadata.case_name: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016

corpus.text: Statutory Text - Section 53, Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code 2016: 'Distribution of assets: (1) Notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in any law enacted by the Parliament or any State Legislature for the time being in force, the proceeds from the sale of the liquidation assets shall be distributed in the following order of priority: (a) insolvency resolution process costs and liquidation costs; (b) debts owed to a secured creditor who has relinquished security and workmen's dues for twenty-four months; (c) wages and unpaid dues owed to employees other than workmen; (d) financial debts owed to unsecured creditors; (e) taxes owed to the Central Government and State Government.'

metadata.case_name: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016

corpus.text: In Union of India v. Mohit Minerals Pvt. Ltd. (2022) 10 SCC 700, the Supreme Court struck down Central Government notifications levying Integrated Goods and Services Tax (IGST) on ocean freight paid by foreign exporters under CIF (Cost, Insurance, and Freight) contracts under the reverse charge mechanism. The court held that under Section 2(30) and Section 8 of the CGST Act, CIF contracts constitute a single indivisible composite supply where transportation is bundled with the supply of goods. Taxing ocean freight separately violates the composite supply statutory mandate. The court also held that GST Council recommendations under Article 279A are non-binding and possess persuasive value only.

metadata.case_name: Union of India v. Mohit Minerals Pvt. Ltd.

corpus.text: In Union of India v. Bharti Airtel Ltd. (2022) 4 SCC 328, the Supreme Court overturned a Delhi High Court decision and held that registered taxpayers under the CGST Act 2017 cannot unilaterally alter or rectify monthly return Form GSTR-3B for past tax periods to claim cash refunds of excess Input Tax Credit (ITC). The court held that Form GSTR-2A is an informational ledger rather than a statutory document conferring a right to unilateral return amendment outside the self-assessment statutory cycle.

metadata.case_name: Union of India v. Bharti Airtel Ltd.

corpus.text: In Radha Krishan Industries v. State of Himachal Pradesh (2021) 6 SCC 771, the Supreme Court set aside an order of provisional attachment of bank accounts under Section 83 of the Himachal Pradesh GST / CGST Act. The court held that provisional attachment is a draconian power that severely hampers business operations; it cannot be exercised routinely or speculatively. The Commissioner must form an independent, objective opinion based on tangible material showing provisional attachment is necessary to protect government revenue.

metadata.case_name: Radha Krishan Industries v. State of H.P.

corpus.text: In Vodafone International Holdings B.V. v. Union of India (2012) 6 SCC 613, a three-judge bench of the Supreme Court held that the offshore transfer of shares of an overseas holding company (CGP Investments, Cayman Islands) between non-residents was not taxable in India under Section 9(1)(i) of the Income Tax Act 1961, even though CGP indirectly held a controlling 67% equity interest in Hutchison Essar Ltd in India. The court affirmed the 'look at' principle versus the 'look through' principle, holding that tax authorities cannot disregard legitimate corporate structures unless established to be fraudulent or sham devices.

metadata.case_name: Vodafone International Holdings v. UOI

corpus.text: In A.K. Kraipak v. Union of India (1969) 2 SCC 262, a five-judge Constitution Bench held that the dividing line between an administrative power and a quasi-judicial power is quite thin and being gradually obliterated. The court ruled that principles of natural justice, specifically the rule against bias (nemo judex in causa sua), apply equally to administrative bodies. An acting Chief Conservator of Forests who was himself a candidate for selection to the Indian Forest Service acted on the selection board; the selections were quashed because real likelihood of bias existed.

metadata.case_name: A.K. Kraipak v. Union of India

corpus.text: Statutory Text - Section 2(30), Central Goods and Services Tax Act 2017: ''composite supply' means a supply made by a taxable person to a recipient consisting of two or more taxable supplies of goods or services or both, or any combination thereof, which are naturally bundled and supplied in conjunction with each other in the ordinary course of business, one of which is a principal supply;'

metadata.case_name: Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017

corpus.text: Statutory Text - Section 8, Central Goods and Services Tax Act 2017: 'Tax liability on composite and mixed supplies: The tax liability on a composite or a mixed supply shall be determined in the following manner, namely:— (a) a composite supply comprising two or more supplies, one of which is a principal supply, shall be treated as a supply of such principal supply; and (b) a mixed supply comprising two or more supplies shall be treated as a supply of that particular supply which attracts the highest rate of tax.'

metadata.case_name: Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017

corpus.text: Statutory Text - Section 83, Central Goods and Services Tax Act 2017: 'Provisional attachment to protect revenue in certain cases: (1) Where, after the initiation of any proceeding under Chapter XII, Chapter XIV or Chapter XV, the Commissioner is of the opinion that for the purpose of protecting the interest of the Government revenue it is necessary so to do, he may, by order in writing, attach provisionally any property, including bank account, belonging to the taxable person.'

metadata.case_name: Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017
